The bank has 25 zonal offices, which are located all over India.{{Cite web|url=https://punjabandsind.bank.in/content/zonal-offices|title=Zonal Offices|website=punjabandsind.bank.in/}} ==History== [[File:Photograph of S. Tarlochan Singh, Bhai Vir Singh, and Sir Sundar Singh Majithia, founders of Punjab & Sind Bank, 1907.jpg|thumb|Punjab & Sind Bank founders group portrait. From left-to-right: Tarlochan Singh, [[Vir Singh (writer)|Vir Singh]], [[Sundar Singh Majithia]], 1907]] The first branch of the bank in [[Amritsar]] was established on 24 June 1908 by [[Sikhs|Sikh]] reformers of the [[Singh Sabha movement]], namely [[Vir Singh (writer)|Bhai Vir Singh]], [[Sundar Singh Majithia|Sir Sunder Singh Majitha]], and Sardar Tarlochan Singh, to serve the then [[Sind Division|Sind]] and [[Punjab Province (British India)|Punjab]] areas of [[British Raj|colonial India]].{{Cite web|url=https://punjabandsind.bank.in/content/history1|title=History|website=punjabandsind.bank.in/}}{{Cite web |last=Singh |first=Kanika |date=15 December 2025 |title=How illustrated calendars issued by the Punjab and Sind Bank became an archive of Sikh history |url=https://scroll.in/article/1089283/how-illustrated-calendars-issued-by-the-punjab-and-sind-bank-became-an-archive-of-sikh-history |access-date=17 May 2026 |website=Scroll.in}}Singh, Kanika. “Punjab & Sind Bank and the Creation of Sikh Heritage.” ''The Story of a Sikh Museum: Heritage, Politics, Popular Culture''. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2025. Print. Retrieved on 16 May 2026 from: https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/story-of-a-sikh-museum/punjab-sind-bank-and-the-creation-of-sikh-heritage/DD9546B509EB1117E57E4E54CB3FE3D3{{Reference page|pages=17–18}} The bank was established as a bank "by the Sikhs, for the Sikhs". The bank initially was going to be named ''The Punjab Union Bank Ltd'' but it ended being incorporated as ''The Punjab & Sind Bank Limited'' to accommodate the Punjabi population living in Sindh. It opened on 24 June 1908 at Hall Bazaar, Amritsar with an ''[[Akhand Path|akhand path]]'' and ''[[Ardās|ardas]]'' prayer by Mohan Singh, with 10,000 rupees being collected for the bank on its first opening. Majithia was the chairman for the Board of Directors, Trilochan Singh was the managing director, and the other directors were Vir Singh, Dharam Singh, Mahindar Singh, Harkishan Lal, Mehr Singh Chawla, Baghail Singh, and Shivdev Singh.{{Reference page|pages=17–18}} Two other branches were opened shortly after, namely at Gujranwala (August 1908) and Rawalpindi (October 1908).{{Reference page|pages=19–20}} By 1947, the bank had eleven branches at Amritsar, Lahore, Lyallpur, Gujranwala, Rawalpindi City, Rawalpindi Cantt, Sialkot and Ludhiana, with sub-offices in Jaranwala, Lahore City and Gojra. However, the [[Partition of India|1947 partition of India]] led to it losing many of its locations in the newly-formed Pakistan, leaving it with two branches remaining in independent India. The following period of the bank was under [[Balbir Singh (scholar)|Balbir Singh]] (brother of Vir Singh) as its managing director from January 1947 to October 1974. The following year it eight branches after opening new locations and thirteen branches by 1954. In 1960, [[Inderjit Singh (banker)|Inderjit Singh]] joined the bank, becoming chairman in 1968, and managing director between 1980 and 1981. Inderjit Singh's tenure was a period of expansion for the bank, as they had opened 546 new branches between 1968 and 1981. Inderjit Singh introduced a lot of programs in the bank related to Sikh history as he wished to promote Sikh teachings and considered the bank to be "only banking institution for the Sikhs in the country".{{Reference page|pages=19–20}} In the 1960s, Punjab & Sind Bank established a branch in London. The logo of the bank was designed by the artist [[Bodhraj (artist)|Bodhraj]] in 1972.{{Reference page|page=28}} In 1974, it published its first annual calendar on Sikh history. On 15 April 1980, Punjab & Sind Bank was among six banks that the Government of India nationalised in the second wave of nationalisation (the first wave had been in 1969 when the government nationalised the top 14 banks). In 1991 [[Bank of Baroda]] acquired Punjab & Sind Bank's London branch at the behest of the [[Reserve Bank of India]] following Punjab & Sind's involvement in the Sethia fraud in 1987. Since 2004, the bank has shown growth of over 40% year on year, and its IPO was oversubscribed by more than 50 times. On 16 July 2019, Punjab & Sind Bank disclosed that it detected a fraud, worth {{INRConvert|238|c|0}} by the [[Bhushan Power & Steel]] Limited.{{cite news |title=Punjab & Sind Bank flags fraud in Bhushan Power account |url=https://www.livemint.com/companies/news/punjab-sind-bank-flags-fraud-in-bhushan-power-account-1563371557452.html |publisher=[[Livemint]] |date=17 July 2019}} == Products== The Capital Adequacy Ratio (Basel III) of the Bank is 12.76% as on 31.03.2020. == Patronage of Sikh art == In independent India, bodies commissioning new [[Sikh art|Sikh artwork]] tended to be Sikh museums (with their resident artist), private organisations (chiefly P&S Bank), and the government. These three sources of Sikh art patronage frequently overlapped with one another due to individuals being involved in more than one source, thus are described as "intersecting threads of patronage" by Kanika Singh. Beginning in 1974 under the guise of Inderjit Singh, Makhan Singh, and Satbir Singh, the Punjab & Sind Bank hired artists to create artwork based on Sikh heritage for its annually published illustrated calendar. Some of the artists hired to create artwork for the bank's calendar included [[Devender Singh]], [[Mehar Singh (artist)|Mehar Singh]], [[Bodhraj (artist)|Bodhraj]], [[Kirpal Singh (artist)|Kirpal Singh]], [[R. M. Singh|Rahi Mohinder Singh]], [[Jarnail Singh (artist)|Jarnail Singh]], and Amolak Singh. These paintings were created to promote the teachings of the Sikh gurus and inform the younger generations. Sometimes a calendar issue and its associated artwork was dedicated to a specific topic, such as the 1975 issue covering historical Sikh women while the 1976 issue was based on ''[[Kirtan|kirtaniyas]]'', specifically historical Sikh musicians. Sometimes a historical event from Sikh history was first-ever depicted in the P&D Bank's calendar art. In 1980, the formerly private bank was nationalised by the government of India but it continued to publish illustrated Sikh calendar artwork with commissioned works until the early 2000s, after which paintings in its calendars were replaced with photographs. The artwork created for the bank's calendar was later donated on the initiative of Harbans Singh to the [[Bhai Mati Das Museum]] in New Delhi.{{Cite journal |last=Singh |first=Kanika |date=9 April extract: Punjab & Sind Bank is an Indian public sector bank headquartered in New Delhi. As of 30 June 2025, the bank has 1817 branches, which are widely spread across India.
